claimBlocks.suggestedSection: A San Carlos account of land and forced change
claimBlocks.text: The San Carlos Apache Tribe’s history describes seasonal movement between river valleys and higher country, linking planting, gathering and hunting with a varied landscape. It then recounts settler encroachment, confinement and assimilation policies that disrupted those relationships. Its schooling account describes separation from families and suppression of language and cultural practices. This community narrative provides a particular historical perspective; it does not establish one identical experience for every Apache people.

claimBlocks.suggestedSection: Two distinct peoples within the Yavapai-Apache Nation
claimBlocks.text: The Yavapai-Apache Nation’s own introduction identifies Yavapai and Apache as two distinct peoples and gives separate self-names and language affiliations. It locates the nation through five communities in Arizona’s Verde Valley. A shared government therefore should not flatten those identities into one interchangeable ethnic label. This concise primary page supplies orientation; its population figures are explicitly dated 2019, and its undated services list is not a verified current inventory.
claimBlocks.sourceLocator: Introduction and identity paragraphs, lines 15–17; scope of service list 21–31

claimBlocks.text: Tonto Apache Community School’s account dates its establishment to 2023 and describes community control over curriculum and cultural learning. It also presents an early-learning program alongside primary and elementary education. These are the institution’s own formation history and stated aims. They provide a local educational example, rather than proof of present enrolment, learning outcomes, unchanged staffing or a single school system shared by all Apache nations.

countAndScopeNotes: One substantive history plus two primary supporting orientations; do not promote short pages merely to reach four. All three proposed claim blocks cite the actual inspected works.
Renew San Carlos history and Yavapai-Apache baseline cards rather than adding duplicate cards for the same URLs. The unresolved language URL must remain navigable without a false new review date.
San Carlos history and Tonto school statements are different works with different community scope. Neither can describe every Western Apache or all Apache-speaking people.

Yavapai and Apache remain distinct peoples within the Yavapai-Apache Nation. The Payson-area Tonto Apache Tribe and its school are separate institutional subjects. A related self-name does not prove governmental equivalence.
